summary:
1. Summary 

The CLPS Lunar Mission Browser is a free, offline web app that shows when sunlight and Earth line-of-sight are available at any lunar landing site on any date. A lunar night lasts about 14 Earth days, and near the poles the Sun skims the horizon. Moving a lander only 5 km east can cut the Sun’s elevation from 10.66° to 6.76° and lengthen the longest night by 66 hours. Scheduling a landing is therefore a survival decision.

Our tool turns NASA lunar terrain and ephemeris data into a “light calendar”. Users pick a site, pick dates, and read a verdict covering Sun, Earth link, power, heat and cost. It scores 160 sites in one pass and maps 20 brief requirements. In the IM-2 Athena example, starting 5 days earlier cuts the longest night from 330 h to 174 h.

Everything runs in the browser with no servers. It is built on NASA LRO/LOLA data and the MIT-licensed LunaHorizon engine, and its ephemeris agrees with JPL Horizons to within 0.0007°. We publish what we get wrong: 100 audited limitations, including a planning-grade terrain mask south of 75.5°S.

The goal is to help planners, students and mission teams make faster, more transparent landing-window decisions.
details:
What it does: The browser app computes Sun elevation, Earth visibility, longest-night duration and the resulting power, thermal and cost trade-offs for any site and date. Users pick a site, pick dates, and read the verdict. It checks 160 sites in one pass.

Benefits: Planners see how a small change in location or start date affects survival. In the IM-2 Athena example, a 5-day earlier start cuts the longest night from 330 h to 174 h. It is free, works offline and needs no servers.

Intended impact: We want to make landing-site and schedule decisions faster, more transparent and accessible to students, professors and mission teams.

Tools: A static web app with 12 modules, built on NASA LRO/LOLA terrain data and JPL ephemeris values. It uses 187 bundled values, 50 linked archives and the MIT-licensed LunaHorizon engine. Zero-invariant checks keep the physics consistent.

Creativity: We turned lunar illumination into a “Moon’s light calendar” that anyone can use in a browser. We also publish our own errors in an audit of 100 limitations.

Factors considered: Accuracy (Sun position within 0.0007° of the ephemeris), the planning-grade terrain mask south of 75.5°S, clarity for every skill level, offline use, and honesty that we are not endorsed by NASA.
